item.title: What makes a good bachata lesson?
item.content:encoded:
By now I've been to a total of 30+ bachata lessons at 4 different studios in 2 countries. So I've decided to write down some of the features of what makes a good - as well as bad - bachata lesson.

Let's start with the good:

  • Enough time to practice. By far, practice is the most important factor of whether I actually learn something or not. Bachata (and other pair dances) are unique in that they aren't really practicable alone at home. So having sufficient practice in class is crucial. As for socials, typically they aren't a good place to do new moves since it won't look great (and I'll embarass my partner), however, if other students in my class are in the same social, I get a lot of practice time with them, then that's good. This is why I try to stack lessons with socials immediately after.
  • Getting to dance with the teachers. In classes I'm typically rotating with other students who are also learning, so neither of us really know what the "correct" way is. However, when teachers join the rotation, it's really useful for us all as an "anchor" to a source of correctness.
  • Low student teacher ratio. This one's pretty straightforward; more teachers means more eyeballs, and more correction.
  • Naming. Name your moves! All of human knowledge is taxonomizing and naming; dance moves are no different. Names give us handles by which we can recall moves and discuss them with people. Examples: around-the-world, lateral hip roll, sliding door.

Now the bad:

  • Excessively pedantry, particularly second-by-second granularity. At timescales shorter than a second, I don't find instructions useful, since bachata music, indeed any kind of latin dance music, happens way too fast for that to be useful. All the minutiae goes out the window at the speed of a real dance. Better to focus on getting it right at realistic timescales.
  • Showy-off teachers. I've had teachers who "show off": they do some complicated set of moves when showing us what they want to teach, then ask us to "copy" that bit that they really wanted to teach us. If you don't wanna teach the move, don't show it! You'll only confuse your students.

Here's a laundry list of other little things to note:

  • Space: sufficient space for the number of students
  • Air conditioning: small rooms get hot quickly when you stuff them full of people moving around
  • Familiar songs: really useful for learning since the music doesn't change

item.title: You should join a book club
item.content:encoded:
Like most people these days, I too, carry around a little attention sucking brick in my pocket. As a result my attention span has almost certainly been permanently damaged. I admit, I've been fully Instagram Reels pilled - it's a good product! - much to the chagrin of my former book loving self.

Which is kind of ironic, since I also happen to run a book club. You'd think that I'd be a reading enthusiast already. But the truth is, I'm not - I'm just like the rest of you.

I do want to be though! And I happen to like organizing things. So what I found is that, running a book club itself can help me read, by providing external motivation to do so. I'm the kind of person who needs someone to push me to do things, so this happens to work out well for me.

For most of us, we get our external motivations first from our parents, then school, then work. But outside of these venues, we... don't really have anything to drive us in a particular direction.

(I mean, another way to look at this is as freedom/"free time", but most people really spend it doomscrolling anyways. Is that really freedom?)

The point is, external motivations work. So join a book club today, even if you don't currently read. All it requires is that you want to. Don't doomscroll your dreams away.

item.title: How I journal
item.content:encoded:
So I've been journaling for a while now and I figured it'd be helpful to write down how I do it, in case this helps anyone else.

For context, I've been doing this on and off for the last five years. While I try to write every day, realistically, it's closer to every few days. Sometimes I miss entire weeks. But that's fine: this is your personal journal, you can write it however you like, whenever you like, as long as you write in the end, it'll be beneficial. Any amount of writing is better than no writing.

In terms of the actual medium that I write on, I have the following hard requirements

  • Private: this rules out physical journals, unless I also get a physical safe and lock it up, but that seems too tedious
  • Searchable: valuable to be able to Ctrl-F a particular keyword
  • Simple: no distracting nonsense

You probably have heard of the note taking app Notion, which is what I started with, which did the job well. However since 2023 their product has't really improved and in fact degraded, specifically, enshittified. For example they never bothered implementing password protected notes, a top requested feature on their own subreddit. The last straw for me was their attempt to shove AI down their users' throats (Press Space for AI) which made the app annoyingly unusable. Maybe this is surprising for the folks at Notion, but I want to press Space for Space, not for AI, especially when it comes to my own freakin' journal. Either way, Notion isn't even a note taking app anymore, and I've since moved off it.

My current workflow is just to jot everything down in one large markdown file which I read from and write to with Obsidian. This is the simplest setup I can think of and it works remarkably well. I simply keep prepending entries to the top. Obsidian has a ton of plugins, of these I use the encryption plugins and Obsidian Sync (a paid product), and nothing else. You'd think that the file size would be a problem, but so far I'm at 50,000 words and 375Kb. For most computers purchased in the last ten years this is not a problem.

item.title: Retatrutide
item.content:encoded:
The weight loss drug revolution continues!

First we had single receptor, GLP-1 agnostists (Semaglutide, "Ozempic"). Then we had double receptor, GLP-1 and GIP agonists (Tirzepatide). Now we have triple receptor agonists: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon (Retatrutide). And they're better than ever!

I don't claim to be an expert here, but my very simplified, high level understanding is:

  • GLP-1 agonists help you lose weight, by reducing your appetite
  • GIP agonists help you to regulate blood sugar, and somehow enhances the weight loss effect of GLP-1
  • Glucagon agonists help you burn more calories

So, with retatrutide, we have both decreased energy intake and increased energy expenditure. Great!

Even though these drugs are in varying stages of medical approval, the headline numbers seem quite promising: semaglutide already helps reduce weight by about 15% after 68 weeks, while retatrutide goes even further up to 25%. Besides that, there are a bunch of promising-but-not-fully-checked benefits such as: reduced risk of Alzheimer's, reduction of knee arthritis pain, better cardio health, etc.

The miracle drug is upon us.

item.title: Simulation Argument
item.content:encoded:
The most convincing argument I've heard in favor of theism so far is the Simulation Argument.

But first, we need to talk about ancestor simulations. Simply put, an ancestor simulation is us, but in the future! To our faraway descendants, we will be their ancestors, and just like how we today are interested in how the cavemen lived, so too will our descendants will be interested in how we lived.

A key property of these ancestor simulations is that they are actually legitimate conscious experiences - the very same kind of consciousness you are experiencing right now - and not some watered down video game version. The real stuff. This means that we need to believe that consciousness can exist on things other than biological brains. Perhaps silicon chips?

(This is called substrate independence, the idea that experiences like consciousness can exist independently of their physical forms. Numbers, for instance. But not everyone buys this!)

Okay, with that, the Simulation Argument goes something like this:

  1. Future civilizations can run many ancestor simulations.
  2. Future civilizations will run many ancestor simulations.
  3. Therefore, it is likely that we are currently in an ancestor simulation.

So: if our descendants become technologically advanced enough to run such simulations, and they in fact do so, many times, simulating entire universes over and over again, then the number of simulated consciousnesses would likely be several orders of magnitude higher than biological ones. And so we're probably in one right now!

Okay, so there are several parts of this argument that can be contested.

(1) may not come true for several reasons: perhaps all civilizations may hit technological barrier eventually. Perhaps we will always hit civilization ending nuclear war, or AI catastrophe, that sets us back to square one. Perhaps it's just too difficult!

As for (2): perhaps future humans may find it evil to run ancestor simulations, which, after all, are supposedly so real! Or maybe they're just not interested enough to find out how we lived.

Finally, if we are in an ancestor simulation, then our simulators are to us as we are to The Sims...

Either way, even though this doesn't quite tip me past the 50% mark of p(theism is true), it does get me pretty close.

item.title: Learning two things at once
item.content:encoded:
A while ago, on the advice of an older engineer who told me about the importance of preventing wrist pain, I bought a ZSA Voyager keyboard.

At the same time, I decided to learn the Colemak-dh keyboard layout. Partly for ergonomic reasons (it's actually easier on the fingers), but mostly because I wanted to see if I could rewire my brain on a tool I've been using practically my whole adult life.

Obviously, this made the switch to the split keyboard twice as difficult. But I figured that I'd get over the pain for both in one go, and perhaps it'd be useful for my brain to have a "trigger" to switch between the layouts: split keyboard + Colemak-dh, laptop + QWERTY.

So for a while, my routine was: start my day with the split keyboard, try to send some messages with it (at a painfully slow 30 wpm), struggle for maybe thirty minutes, then switch to my regular laptop keyboard. This lasted for approximately two weeks. Then I put away the split keyboard in a drawer and promptly forgot about it for the next six months.

Then one day I saw it and remembered, "oh yeah I spent $300 on that", and pulled it out again. For whatever reason - maybe the Colemak neurons in my brain settled? - the second time was much better. When I hit roughly 60-70 wpm, I crossed the threshold where it could become my default layout, then I finally updated my laptop keyboard to match, thus completing the cutover. End to end, this took roughly a year.

So yeah. Split keyboards are great! Just don't pair the cutover with a layout change too, unless you're like me, and like to torture yourself.

item.title: Letters from Victorian London
item.content:encoded:
Love-letter from a Gentleman to a Lady. The Temple, June 4th, circa 1870.

DEAREST,

  Days have passed by now since we have had the pleasure of a few moments' conversation even; how these hours have dragged their slow pace along you and I alone can tell. It is only when we are left to the peaceful enjoyment of our own society that time flies. It may be that to-morrow at Mrs. E.'s we shall have a little time alone. We all dine there; she told me she should have a dance also, and that your mamma had promised her your sister and yourself should be of the party. May I ask for the first waltz? I send a few flowers, but I imagine you will only wear one, the rose in your hair; your sister is always pleased with a bouquet, so I shall not be very angry if you let her have them, only wear my rose.

  Your own
    EDWARD.

Invitation to a Friend. The Elms, August 6th, circa 1870.

MY DEAR ELEANOR,

  I should be very glad if you could come and spend a month with us; the country is really so lovely during hay––making time, and the evenings so deliciously cool, that such an admirer of nature, would, I think, enjoy the change from your wild, rocky scenery to our quiet peaceful valley, and from the roar of the waves to the music of murmuring brooks.
  I expect my brother and sister to spend the autumn with me, and if you can make up your mind to leave home for a short time, they, as well as I, will be delighted with your company. George, who is as merry and mischievous as ever, will, I know, do his utmost to add to your enjoyment, and make your visit a pleasant one.

  With kindest regards to all at home,
    Believe me,
      Your sincere friend,
        ANNIE LEIGHTON.

In 1840, Victorian London saw the introduction of the world's first postal stamp: the Penny Black.

Priced at a single cent (USD 60c today), the Penny Black made sending letters cheaper and simpler. Before, letters were expensive, post-paid and billed by distance, which put it out of reach as a means of communication for most ordinary Victorians. The Penny Black changed that. All of a sudden, everyone could send letters to each other. Within a year, mail volume within the UK doubled.

Reading these letters has been quite fasinating. The first thing that stand out to me is the prose. Just look its length and elaborateness; the Victorians really knew how to stretch out a dinner invitation into a three-part novella. Who knew an invitation could be written so poetically?

The next thing I noticed, while reading the text, is just how different it feels. I've never written anything like that before. Maybe I could, but modern texting standards reserve prose of such length to things like confessions or breakup messages.

How are letters different from other forms of personal, remote communications?

Today, texting dominates, but the brevity of it doesn't really allow for ideas to breathe. Emails exist, but 1. the spam problem makes it impossible for regular people to treat email as a network for serious writing, and 2. emails crucially can be edited. Letters, written on paper, could be edited, but it doesn't quite have the same malleability as electronic text. In that sense letters much closer to a raw streams of thought than anything electronic.

And of course: letters can contain drawings and illustrations!

So if you have several minutes to spare today, I implore you to take a look through the Victorian Letters. In them you shall, I hope, experience the thoughtfulness and kindness in the lives of everyday Victorians. As for myself, I shall be writing more letters to my valued friends, whom I cherish very dearly much.

Yours, ever sincerely,
  -

item.title: Why does food taste better in Asia?
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever wondered why food tastes better in Asia?

Yes, the ingredients here are better. We use more spices, more chili perhaps. Something something more "umami". Some just say that Asians are better at cooking (perhaps a circular claim)?

But I think one commonly underrated factor is the climate.

Many of Asia's big cities are hot and humid. Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong and Tokyo all have so-called humid subtropical climate, while Singapore is straight up tropical.

If you've visited one of these cities before, you probably remember being hit with a wave of humidity on touchdown.

Heat and humidity can intensify the smells around us. Since smell is such an important part of the flavor of food, I wonder if the climate itself makes eating here more enjoyable.

This may also help explain why open air hawking is so prevelant in Asia. Think of the night markets of Taipei or the hawker centers of Singapore. You can often smell the food before you see it. Perhaps the climate makes these places especially effective at drawing in hungry people.

Of course, this effect cuts both ways.

If good things smell better, bad things smell worse. Organic waste decomposes faster, which might explain why uncollected garbage smells awful in these cities!

item.title: Altantuyaa Shaariibuu
item.content:encoded:
The case of Altantuyaa Shaariibuu is just so fascinating. To me it's a little window into the wild world of Malaysian politics, where an event like this is but a blip in the background of someone as important as the Prime Minister of Malaysia.

To quickly summarize: Altantuya was a Mongolian model/translator who back in 2006 worked for one of Najib's close associates, back when Najib was only Deputy PM. Until one day she was found blown up in a Kuala Lumpar parking lot with C4, by Najib's police bodyguards. This case has so many twists and turns and till this day it is not known why she was murdered.

I hope that one day they finally resolve it and we can see a movie about this.

item.title: Cesare Borgia
item.content:encoded:
In The Prince, Machiavelli writes about Cesare Borgia, whose court he had served in as a Florentine diplomat.

Cesare Borgia was a talented Italian statesman/general/warlord during the Renaissance. In 1503, Borgia had already conquered large portions of the Papal States, and was about to round up his conquests with Tuscany, when a series of unfortunate events brought him down.

First Borgia and his father, Pope Alexander VI, attended the same dinner where they both fell extremely ill. Borgia was bedridden, and his father died shortly after. Amidst the chaos, he was unable to consolidate his influence to over the College of Cardinals, the body appointing the next pope.

Though bedridden, Borgia didn't immediately lose all his influence; his loyalists managed to get Pope Pius III, a compromised candidate, elected. However, this proved to be short lived as Pius was already old and ill, and died just two weeks later. (Some of his opponents may have voted for Pius because of that.)

Subsequently, Cardinal Della Rovere approached Borgia with a deal, to get elected in exchange for protecting Borgia. In his weakened state, Borgia accepted, and in 1503 Della Rovere - now Pope Julius II - was elected.

That however - as Machiavelli calls it - was Borgia's "biggest mistake". In fact, Julius was a bitter enemy of the Borgias, dating all the way back to his rivalry with Alexander VI over the papacy in 1492, and he had not forgetten about it.

Immediately upon election, Julius broke all his promises to Borgia and had him arrested. Borgia subsequently fled to Navarre where he died later in battle.

Machiavelli's lesson was that Borgia should have never let someone with such longstanding greviances against him acquire so much power, regardless of the promises that man may have made:

"Whoever believes that among great personages new benefits make old injuries be forgotten deceives himself."

Borgia helped make Julius pope, believing that this would secure his loyalty. Instead, he had handed his greatest enemy the power to destroy him.

item.title: Learning bachata
item.content:encoded:
A few years ago, my roommate dragged me into a bachata dance lesson. I'd never done any kind of dancing before. In fact, I hardly regarded myself as a artsy person at all.

However, something inside me poked at me to try, so I went.

The first lesson I was scared shitless. Bachata is a partner dance, which meant that I had to hold my partner at arm's length for the whole dance (2-3 mins). That was something I was extremely not used to! Additionally, as the lead, I had to, well, lead, to constantly think of the next move, to ensure smooth transitions. I even stressed out about where to look! (Where do I look? At my partner? Above? At the wall?) I never quite got used to it and after my first class package was up, I did not sign up for second one.

A few years later, I'm not sure how but I got the itch to try something new again, and this time I tried to learning bachata for real.

I started by going for both bachata and salsa lessons simultaneously, by myself. Salsa is a faster and more complicated bachata, with an even steeper learning curve. I only ever did the beginner levels, however, it was useful for overcoming nerves, getting used to latin dances in general, and the fact that it was harder made bachata feel easier. Eventually I got much better at bachata (at least I was way less stressed while dancing) and by now I've been to perhaps a dozen or so social dances. Not bad!

Every now and then I get the urge to try something new and put myself out of my comfort zone. It did take a little nudging but I'm glad that I tried dancing and I hope that this inspires someone else to try something new too.

item.title: Differences in dentists
item.content:encoded:
Something that I recently realized is that there are good dentists and bad dentists. That "dentist" is just a binary label; within dentists, like in most disciplines, there is a whole quality spectrum.

I found that out when I switched over to my new, current dentist, who informed me that I was supposed to get bitewing x-rays (the cannon looking one) once a year. My previous dentist did not. So I had not done one in a long time, and when I did, we discovered a hidden decay between two of my molars that had eluded previous visual inspections.

It can be scary to worry about the variance in quality between individual providers, when we cannot pick them, say like your pilot, or your surgeon. But I'm sure that e.g. pilots who graduated at the tenth percentile fly all the time, and I'm sure I've taken one of those flights before, and we're all fine. Perhaps this is testament to the pilot qualification system? Either way, I'm grateful that these systems exist.

item.title: Why am I a theist?
item.content:encoded:
Imagine you're living in a fancy house. One foggy morning, you look out of your window toward your driveway. You see something large, that kinds of resembles a car, but you're not quite sure.

The next words out of your mouth are:

  • A: "it's a car"
  • B: "it's a 2007 Toyota Outback Series 6 with red trim, black leather seats, and a pair of Birkenstocks in the backseat"

Which do you pick?

item.title: No adults in the room
item.content:encoded:
A gradual realization everyone has as they grow up is the fact that there is, in fact, no one in charge. If you find in the position of asking who's in charge, more often than not, its you.

I'd guess that for most people they make this observation first with their parents. Parents, as they are, come with a sense of invincibility. But as you grow up, you start seeing cracks. Of knowledge, of ability. Until the cracks grow into chasms, then you wonder how did they ever make it out of their childhood.

Parenting is hard, and most parents are just "figuring it out", just like most people in most endavors. I find that I have to constantly remind myself about this, especially when I'm at new events meeting people.

item.title: Benzoyl peroxide is acne prevention, not treatment
item.content:encoded:
Most marketing for acne cream is wrong.

What is acne, actually? "Acne" is really two things: the bacterium C. acnes, and the medical condition acne vulgaris. Untreated C. acnes causes acne vulgaris, aka "pimples", "spots".

Most acne cream is made up of benzoyl peroxide. BP works by oxidizing the surface of the skin, effectively killing off C. acnes. Crucially, this means that BP must be applied before acne forms.

However, that is not how most acne creams are marketed! Neutrogena, for instance, markets their On-the-Spot Acne Treatment, 2.5% BP as, well, "spot treatment". But that is the wrong framing. Spot treatment is a misnomer! By the time the acne has shown up, its too late.

Neutrogena is not alone here - there's a whole marketing category of "spot treatments" (e.g. Oxy, 5% BP), which exists for reasons I do not understand. I suspect most people do not empirically evaluate the effectiveness of their acne treatments, or they falsely correlate the natural resolution of their spots with application of acne cream.

Either way: BP prevents acne, so the right way to use it is to apply it at all acne prone areas, before the acne has shown up. For most people this will be the whole face, and for others, the neck, ears, chest, etc.
